1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.background: The 1886 World Championship match between Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort introduced the first modern ideas: Steinitz gave the pawn back and left White with an isolated d4-pawn. Alexander Alekhine added new ideas, and the line was played at the highest level from the 1930s. It declined after the Second World War as the Indian Defences gained ground, but several elite players returned to it in the late 1990s, and it is currently considered sound.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3.strategy: The classical main line: develops a piece, guards d4 and takes the e5 square away, so Black cannot strike at the centre with the e-pawn. White regains the pawn at leisure with the bishop and keeps a flexible, comfortable game against Black's counterplay.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Normal Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3.background: The most popular third move, and the point where the main lines begin.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.strategy: Builds the broadest possible centre at once and frees the c1-bishop to develop. The c4-pawn can be recovered later, because Black has no central pawn and must strike at White's pawns quickly or be squeezed. The most ambitious way to answer the pawn grab.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Saduleto Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.background: An old move that became popular again in the 1990s.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.strategy: A quiet way to regain the pawn: it guards d4 and opens the f1-bishop, which takes back on c4 by development rather than by a pawn move. The price is that Black gets time to strike at the centre, and the typical result is an isolated d-pawn for White.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.background: Strong players have often employed it, among them Anatoly Karpov.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Qa4+.strategy: Checks and prepares to win the c4-pawn back with the queen. It works, but the queen stands exposed on the edge of the board, where Black gains time with natural developing moves. Black equalises easily, and White has nothing in the centre to show for the early queen sortie.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Qa4+.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Accelerated Mannheim Variation

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e5.strategy: Strikes back at once, before White's knight can come to f3 to guard d4. Grabbing the pawn with dxe5 backfires, since ...Qxd1+ forces the queens off and costs White castling. Black gets open piece play, and White will probably end up with an isolated d-pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight fights for the centre and watches e4, leaving White to retake the pawn with the bishop. Black accepts that gain of time for sound development and keeps ways to challenge White's centre later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 e5.strategy: The main reply: Black opposes the pawn centre at once and opens the f8-bishop. White has to be exact, since grabbing on e5 or c4 at once goes wrong, and the game becomes open and highly theoretical, with Black fighting for equality in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Hits the e4-pawn at once and invites White to push it, since a pawn on e5 can become a target. Black lets White have space and plays against the centre with active pieces, but has to prove the advanced pawns are overextended.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nf6.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Alekhine System

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nc6.strategy: Pressures d4 with a piece, using the fact that White has no knight on f3 yet to defend it. Black fights for the centre with pieces instead of pawns, in a modern, active set-up that keeps White from building freely.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 Nc6.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Modern Defence

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 c5.strategy: Undermines the base of White's centre with a pawn. If White advances, the position gets a pawn structure where White has space in the centre and Black plays on the queenside, with the pawn on c4 still to be won back.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.strategy: Tries to keep the extra pawn by supporting it. Risky: White attacks the base of the pawn chain, the queenside is loosened, and White's lead in development gives more than enough compensation for the pawn.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Greco Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 b5.background: Rarely seen, though its popularity rose in the 2020s after the discovery of 6...Qb6; 3...e5 remains more popular.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 f5.strategy: Hits the e4-pawn, but weakens the king's diagonal: Qh5+ is check at once, and exf5 takes the f-pawn and opens the position while Black is undeveloped. Black has the extra pawn on c4, but the king pays for it.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4 f5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Schwartz Defence

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops, controls e4 and keeps White from building a pawn centre. The natural move and Black's most common reply: White regains the pawn with the bishop, and Black gets free development and the centre break later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 a6.strategy: A flexible, useful move: it prepares ...b5 to hold the c4-pawn and keeps White's pieces from the b5-square. Black goes for rapid development and the centre, and the game often settles back into the main lines.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and uses the time White needs to regain the pawn to open the game. White has to decide how to meet the pressure on the centre, while Black plays for the freeing break.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 c5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Gunsberg Defence

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares to strike at d4 with the c-pawn. Solid and flexible, but the pawn on e6 shuts in the c8-bishop for now; the pawn on c4 is simply given back.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 Nd7.strategy: Heads for b6 to attack the c4-pawn and supports a later ...e5, but blocks the c8-bishop and is passive. Harmless rather than good, as White develops freely and regains the pawn without trouble.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 Nd7.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Godes Variation

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 b5.strategy: Tries to hold the pawn, but White's a-pawn at once attacks the base of the chain. Black has to shore up the queenside, which weakens it and usually ends in a passive structure. Rarer here than against 3.e4.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Nf3 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Slav Gambit
